name: Self-improvement 'glow-up' content

lead: Glow-up content is the genre of before-and-after videos and posts showing someone's changed appearance, often crediting skincare, fitness, grooming, clothing or procedures. Viewers use them as examples of what is possible and as templates for their own changes.

The chain is seeing the before-and-after, learning the methods credited, then copying changes to your own looks. It is a social-media descendant of the makeover genre, which has long featured in daytime talk shows, personal makeover television series and film. Few published sources study social-media transformation content specifically.

paras: People watch or save transformation posts, note the haircut, skincare routine, clothing or training approach credited, and try them. Many also post their own progress photos to track and share changes over time.

Before-and-after posts are selected and edited, so lighting, angles and timing can account for part of the difference. Related research links social-media exposure to appearance comparison, so some people find the genre motivating and others find it discouraging.

angle.text: Transformation videos and posts show before-and-after changes in clothing, haircuts, skin, fitness or procedures, and viewers use them as templates and motivation for their own changes. The genre is popular; few studies examine it.

lead: Self-improvement 'glow-up' content refers to transformation videos and posts that present a before-and-after change in appearance, often with the methods credited. It is a social-media descendant of the makeover genre, which Wikipedia describes as a radical change in appearance involving clothing, haircuts, cosmetics and sometimes weight loss, plastic surgery or dental work [1].

Makeovers have long featured in daytime talk shows, personal makeover television series and film [1]. Wikipedia's makeover article does not cover social-media transformation content or research on it [1].

paras: Makeover television formats listed on Wikipedia include Queer Eye, What Not to Wear and Extreme Makeover, and makeover plots recur in films from the 1940s onward [1]. Virtual makeover apps now let users preview cosmetics and hairstyles on a photo in real time [1].

No studies found on transformation content as a genre. A related study of a different intervention, a professional photoshoot labelled a 'glow up' for adolescent psychiatric patients, is described under the Glow up entry.
